forces.title: Soaring Demand for Critical Minerals Drives Mining Sector Growth
forces.description: Global demand for critical minerals such as copper, lithium, and nickel is projected to grow significantly through 2040. These materials are the fundamental building blocks for electrification, renewable energy infrastructure, and battery storage solutions, underpinning the expansion of digital and energy systems. This sustained high demand creates a strong tailwind for the mining sector globally, including for UK companies involved in mineral supply chains or advanced material processing.
forces.source_title: Harnessing AI to make mining safer

forces.title: AI and Automation Enhance Mining Safety and Productivity
forces.description: The mining industry, historically hazardous, is leveraging agentic AI tools and automation to improve safety and operational efficiency. Technologies like autonomous drones, IoT-enabled sensors, and AI-powered hazard detection systems are reducing human exposure to risks, optimizing maintenance, and improving response to irregularities. This technological transformation has the potential to redefine safety standards, increase productivity, and create more sustainable mining operations, acting as a significant upside driver.
forces.source_title: Harnessing AI to make mining safer

forces.title: UK Metals Sector Benefits from Stockpiling and Protective Measures
forces.description: The UK metals sector is experiencing improved pricing and trading conditions, with some steel product prices rising by 40-50% since February 2026. This uplift is primarily due to tariffs, quotas, and geopolitical events encouraging stockpiling, which are expected to support market conditions through the second half of the year. These protective measures provide a significant, albeit short-term, tailwind for domestic producers, helping to bolster revenues and mitigate immediate financial pressures.
forces.source_title: September 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: Elevated Costs and Financial Fragility Challenge UK Metals Sector
forces.description: Despite recent pricing improvements, the UK metals sector remains financially fragile and faces persistent cost pressures. Higher logistics, raw material, and energy costs are increasing financing and working-capital requirements for businesses. Europe, including the UK, continues to lag other regions in terms of overall sector health. This combination of elevated operational costs and underlying financial vulnerability acts as a significant headwind, limiting long-term recovery and resilience.
forces.source_title: September 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: Risk of Price Correction as Stockpiling Demand Normalizes
forces.description: The current improved pricing in the UK metals sector, driven by tariffs, quotas, and geopolitical events encouraging stockpiling, carries an inherent risk. Once buying patterns normalize and the immediate incentive for stockpiling diminishes, there is a possibility that demand and prices could correct. This potential market adjustment poses a key risk for businesses that have benefited from the current buoyant conditions, requiring careful inventory management and pricing discipline.
forces.source_title: September 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: Government Infrastructure Spending Underpins UK Demand
forces.description: Government infrastructure spending in the UK is providing a crucial floor for economic growth, particularly beneficial for sectors like Metals & Mining that supply foundational materials. Although private sector activity remains weak, this sustained public investment ensures a baseline level of demand for steel, concrete, and other construction-related metals. This creates a supportive tailwind, mitigating some of the broader economic uncertainties and offering consistent project pipelines.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

forces.title: Global Steel Overcapacity from China Compresses Margins
forces.description: The global steel market faces persistent overcapacity, particularly from China, which has significantly ramped up manufacturing. In 2024, global capacity exceeded demand by over 600 million tons, leading to compressed margins for steel producers worldwide. This structural imbalance, where excess supply flows into international markets, creates a strong headwind for the Steel & Ferrous Metals sector, intensifying competitive pressure and limiting opportunities for sustained price recovery.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Steel Industry Fragmentation Driven by Geopolitics and Sustainability
forces.description: The global steel market is undergoing a significant structural shift, moving away from purely cost-driven dynamics towards a more fragmented industry shaped by geopolitics, sustainability considerations, and technological advancements. Regional policies, resource constraints, and environmental mandates are increasingly determining investment patterns and production routes, influencing trade flows and competitive terms. This fragmentation introduces new complexities and necessitates strategic adaptation for industry players, including those in the UK.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Shift Towards Lower-Carbon EAF/DRI Steel Production in Europe
forces.description: Europe is increasingly adopting Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) and Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) technologies for steel production, driven by environmental reasons and decarbonization goals. New investments in countries like Germany and Sweden are focused on DRI-EAF plants, which offer a smaller carbon footprint compared to traditional Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) routes. This shift represents a high-impact structural change, requiring significant investment and reshaping the regional steelmaking landscape.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: EU Carbon Pricing Boosts DRI-EAF Steel Competitiveness
forces.description: The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) is increasing costs for traditional Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) steel production, making Direct Reduced Iron-Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) technologies more attractive. As allowances are phased out, carbon costs penalize higher-emission methods, creating a relative advantage for lower-carbon DRI-EAF plants. This policy-driven mechanism acts as a strong tailwind for investments in green steel production within Europe, although often requiring initial subsidies.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: High European Natural Gas Prices Increase Green Steel Production Costs
forces.description: European steel producers adopting Direct Reduced Iron-Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) technology face a significant cost disadvantage due to high natural gas prices. Natural gas is a critical input for the DRI process, and prices in Europe can be two to five times higher than in regions like Oman or the United States. This pronounced gas cost disadvantage substantially increases the levelized cost of green steel production in Europe, acting as a major headwind for its widespread adoption without significant subsidies.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Cost Advantage of BF-BOF Steel in Asia Hinders Green Transition
forces.description: Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) steel production in India and China offers significantly lower levelized costs compared to Direct Reduced Iron-Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) methods, even in competitive regions like Oman. This cost advantage, driven by access to cheap coal and strong domestic demand, continues to draw investment towards BF-BOF facilities, despite their higher CO2 emissions. This creates a substantial headwind for the global transition to lower-emissions steel, reinforcing traditional production routes.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Trade Policies Support Domestic Steel Production and Investment
forces.description: Global trade policies, including Section 232 tariffs in the United States, EU-27 import quotas and tariffs, and India's domestic preference rules, are increasingly supporting local steel production. These measures raise import prices, encourage domestic manufacturing, and alter regional investment patterns. For UK steel producers, similar protective frameworks or access to markets with such policies can provide a significant tailwind, enhancing competitiveness and ensuring demand for locally produced materials.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism Raises European Steel Prices
forces.description: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is designed to level the playing field by charging carbon pricing on imported steel, but it will also increase the overall price of steel within Europe. This measure adds to the cost burden for European steel users and, by extension, impacts the end-users of metal products in the UK. While aiming to encourage decarbonization, CBAM acts as a headwind by increasing input costs for the Metals & Mining sector and downstream industries.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Supply Constraints for Critical Minerals Amid Rising Global Demand
forces.description: The increasing global demand for critical and transition minerals (e.g., REEs, nickel, manganese, copper, lithium) for energy transition and advanced technologies faces persistent supply constraints. These limitations stem from issues like ore quality, processing inefficiencies, and inadequate infrastructure. Geopolitical conflicts and resource nationalism further disrupt mineral flows and deter investment, posing a high-impact key risk to securing stable and affordable supply chains for the Metals & Mining sector globally and within the UK.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

forces.title: African Mining Faces Structural Challenges and Underinvestment
forces.description: African mining, despite its abundant critical mineral reserves, struggles with structural challenges that erode its geological advantage. These include widespread underinvestment in early-stage mine development and exploration, high country risk, legal and jurisdictional uncertainties, and pervasive infrastructure deficits (roads, rail, power). These factors lead to higher operating costs, deter foreign investment, and impede project progression, creating a significant headwind for global mineral supply chains, including for UK entities sourcing from Africa.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

forces.title: Clustering Mining Assets Enhances Efficiency and Investment Attractiveness
forces.description: Clustering mining operations in geographic proximity, integrating investments, and sharing infrastructure (e.g., ports, processing plants) can significantly improve project economics. This approach can boost ore production volumes by up to 5% and reduce unit costs by approximately 20%. By spreading risk, creating investible ecosystems, and driving in-country value addition, clustering acts as a high-impact upside driver, making projects more attractive to investors and fostering regional development in mineral-rich areas.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

forces.title: Operational Excellence and Capital Efficiency Boost Mining Profitability
forces.description: Streamlining operating costs and optimizing major investments offer significant opportunities to enhance profitability in mining. Strategies such as right-sizing starter projects, phasing development, prioritizing higher-grade ore, and improving planning can reduce capital expenditures by up to 15% and operational expenditures by 20%, while also shortening timelines by a year and improving revenue by 5% through enhanced recovery. These measures represent a high-impact upside driver for mining companies to strengthen their competitive positioning and cash flows.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

forces.title: AI, EVs, and Renewables Drive Sustained Materials Demand
forces.description: The rapid advancement and adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Electric Vehicles (EVs), and renewable energy infrastructure are generating sustained high demand for specific materials, particularly steel, aluminum, and copper. Data center investments, for instance, are expected to reach trillions by 2030, with IT equipment being a dominant driver. This technological revolution creates a powerful and enduring tailwind for the Metals & Mining sector, necessitating higher-quality materials with tighter tolerances.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: Geopolitical Realignment and Reshoring Increase Domestic Materials Demand
forces.description: Geopolitically driven supply chain reorganization, including the reshoring of many industrial processes, is leading to a step change in domestic materials demand. For example, US manufacturing construction spending significantly increased, fueled by investments in semiconductor chip manufacturing and supply chain reshoring. This structural shift towards localized production for resilience, rather than solely cost efficiency, creates a strong tailwind for domestic materials producers, including those in the UK, as demand for local sourcing rises.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: Growing Share of Green Metals in Global Supply Chains
forces.description: The materials supply chain is undergoing a structural transformation with buyers planning to significantly increase the share of green metals from approximately 21% today to 32% by 2030. This shift is driven by decarbonization commitments and evolving material specifications. It creates a powerful tailwind for producers of responsibly sourced and low-carbon metals, necessitating capabilities such as carbon reporting and segregated green flows. This trend pushes the Metals & Mining sector towards more sustainable practices and differentiated product offerings.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

viewpoints.title: UK Metals Sector Sees Short-Term Pricing Improvement Amid Fragility
viewpoints.description: The UK metals sector is experiencing improved short-term trading conditions and better pricing since February 2026. This uplift is driven by tariffs, quotas, and geopolitical events encouraging stockpiling, with some steel product prices increasing by 40-50%. These protective measures are expected to support conditions through the latter half of the year. However, the sector remains financially fragile, with Europe lagging other regions. The outlook suggests a cautious optimism for the near term, but underlying vulnerabilities persist.

viewpoints.title: Mining's Global Role Poised for Growth Driven by Critical Minerals Demand
viewpoints.description: Mining is set for significant global growth as it supplies essential materials for digital and energy infrastructure. Demand for critical minerals like copper, lithium, and nickel, crucial for electrification, renewables, and battery storage, is projected to grow substantially through 2040. Despite the industry's hazardous nature, technological advancements, particularly agentic AI tools, present opportunities to enhance safety and productivity, supporting this expanding role in the global economy.
viewpoints.source_title: Harnessing AI to make mining safer

viewpoints.title: Key Materials Demand in Europe and North America to See Sustained Growth
viewpoints.description: After a decade of flatness (2015-2024), demand for critical industrial materials including steel, aluminum, copper, and stainless steel is projected to return to sustained growth through 2030 in Europe and North America. This acceleration is fueled by geopolitical realignment, reshoring of industrial processes, the push for decarbonization (increasing green metals' share), and new technology engines like AI, EVs, and renewable energy infrastructure.
viewpoints.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

demand_drivers.description: Global demand for energy transition materials, including critical minerals, is projected to grow significantly, fueled by electrification, renewables, and battery storage.

market_sizing.methodology: McKinsey's Global Materials Perspective 2025 estimates demand growth for energy transition materials, driven by global energy and technology transitions.
market_sizing.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

demand_drivers.description: Investment decisions in steel technologies are based on the optimal production route for a given location, influenced by natural gas costs, electricity costs, and raw material availability.

pnl_drivers.description: Energy costs, particularly natural gas for the Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) step, are the main contributor to variations in levelized cost across locations, significantly impacting profitability.
The cost of electricity, especially for powering the Electric Arc Furnace (EAF), varies by location and can add significantly to the levelized cost of steel production.
Carbon pricing, such as under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), adds costs to BF-BOF production, creating a relative advantage for DRI-EAF and influencing investment viability.

market_sizing.methodology: Levelized cost of DRI-EAF hot-rolled coil steel production, calculated using a methodology that converts a project’s full life cycle economics into a single unit cost, excluding taxes, subsidies, and externalities. Costs for specific geographies are benchmarked against Oman as the base case.
market_sizing.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: Growth in the wholesale distribution business is primarily tied to overall materials demand growth across various industrial sectors.

market_sizing.methodology: Market size for wholesale distribution business in Europe and North America, with a forecast CAGR through 2030. This includes material wholesalers connecting mills to manufacturers across industrial sectors.
market_sizing.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

demand_drivers.description: Manufacturers are increasingly outsourcing processing (cutting, slitting, forming) and logistics services to service centers, driving demand for these value-added services.

new_opportunities.description: Service centers are well-positioned to offer processing, customization, and inventory risk management services as OEMs outsource more of these functions.
Complexities arising from tariffs, reshoring, and regionalization are increasing demand for 3PL and 4PL 'control tower' services in materials supply chains.

market_sizing.methodology: Forecast annual expansion rates for materials service centers and finishing/light-assembly services in Europe and North America, driven by OEM outsourcing trends.
market_sizing.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain
